My CODE BLUE 2026 talk "Pass-the-Device" is now public: slides (EN/JA), 5 recon tools, experimental Sigma + KQL detections.
https://t.co/i9GOCnUofD

The idea: device trust is not device binding.

From one compromised, enrolled laptop there are two routes off the host:
A) copy existing state: cert, cookie, client config
B) enroll a new client with the user's SSO
Both end on a machine with no EDR. Each leaves a different record to revoke.

The goal is practical: to know where the trust boundaries are, to know the limits of what your VPN/SASE solution can do, and to understand which configuration you need.

Two real cases, Cisco and Zscaler: host isolated, account disabled, and the second session stayed alive. A fresh VPN/SASE enrollment is persistence outside EDR.

Three checks for defenders this week:
1. Do your VPN/SASE, enrollment and IdP logs reach the SIEM at all?
2. Compare every device enrolled in the last 90 days with your managed-device inventory.
3. Add one line to the IR playbook: end the user's VPN/SASE sessions and revoke the enrollments, not only the host.

Thank you @codeblue_jp.

items.content:
RT @cyb3rops: I think there’s a fundamental misconception in how the security industry talks about ARTEX, Cairn and similar offensive AI frameworks. And even reports from major security vendors keep reinforcing it.

People treat these frameworks like the C2 frameworks we’ve known for years. With Cobalt Strike and others, parts of the framework were deployed on the victim’s systems. Implants, loaders, communication protocols and other implementation details provided recognizable patterns that we could write signatures for.

But ARTEX and Cairn work differently. The orchestration runs on the attacker side. The LLMs, prompts, skills, tools and infrastructure are interchangeable. Change any of these components and the resulting attack can look completely different. The framework itself doesn’t define what ends up on the victim’s systems.

Yes, there are a few minor implementation fingerprints, such as certain ARTEX/Norma User-Agent strings. We’ve even written rules for them. But these cover tiny parts of a framework’s functionality, not the attacks it can orchestrate.

An IP address, webshell or exploit used in a campaign doesn’t suddenly become an “ARTEX indicator” because ARTEX was involved.

And that’s why I find all these “ARTEX IoC collections” and “How to detect ARTEX” guides so misleading. They encourage people to think we’re dealing with another recognizable malware or C2 framework.

We’re facing a different class of offensive technology, and I think many people still haven’t understood that.

The detection guidance should be what we’ve been telling defenders for decades: detect malicious behavior, attack techniques and traces of compromise.

There is no special defense against ARTEX. Tomorrow the same attacker could use a different framework, a different model and completely different tools.

The names are disposable. The underlying attack techniques are what we need to detect.

items.content:
RT @cyb3rops: I think there’s a fundamental misconception in how the security industry talks about ARTEX, Cairn and similar offensive AI frameworks. And even reports from major security vendors keep reinforcing it.

People treat these frameworks like the C2 frameworks we’ve known for years. With Cobalt Strike and others, parts of the framework were deployed on the victim’s systems. Implants, loaders, communication protocols and other implementation details provided recognizable patterns that we could write signatures for.

But ARTEX and Cairn work differently. The orchestration runs on the attacker side. The LLMs, prompts, skills, tools and infrastructure are interchangeable. Change any of these components and the resulting attack can look completely different. The framework itself doesn’t define what ends up on the victim’s systems.

Yes, there are a few minor implementation fingerprints, such as certain ARTEX/Norma User-Agent strings. We’ve even written rules for them. But these cover tiny parts of a framework’s functionality, not the attacks it can orchestrate.

An IP address, webshell or exploit used in a campaign doesn’t suddenly become an “ARTEX indicator” because ARTEX was involved.

And that’s why I find all these “ARTEX IoC collections” and “How to detect ARTEX” guides so misleading. They encourage people to think we’re dealing with another recognizable malware or C2 framework.

We’re facing a different class of offensive technology, and I think many people still haven’t understood that.

The detection guidance should be what we’ve been telling defenders for decades: detect malicious behavior, attack techniques and traces of compromise.

There is no special defense against ARTEX. Tomorrow the same attacker could use a different framework, a different model and completely different tools.

The names are disposable. The underlying attack techniques are what we need to detect.

The idea: device trust is not device binding.

From one compromised, enrolled laptop there are two routes off the host:
A) copy existing state: cert, cookie, client config
B) enroll a new client with the user's SSO
Both end on a machine with no EDR. Each leaves a different record to revoke.

The goal is practical: to know where the trust boundaries are, to know the limits of what your VPN/SASE solution can do, and to understand which configuration you need.

Two real cases, Cisco and Zscaler: host isolated, account disabled, and the second session stayed alive. A fresh VPN/SASE enrollment is persistence outside EDR.

Three checks for defenders this week:
1. Do your VPN/SASE, enrollment and IdP logs reach the SIEM at all?
2. Compare every device enrolled in the last 90 days with your managed-device inventory.
3. Add one line to the IR playbook: end the user's VPN/SASE sessions and revoke the enrollments, not only the host.

But ARTEX and Cairn work differently. The orchestration runs on the attacker side. The LLMs, prompts, skills, tools and infrastructure are interchangeable. Change any of these components and the resulting attack can look completely different. The framework itself doesn’t define what ends up on the victim’s systems.

Yes, there are a few minor implementation fingerprints, such as certain ARTEX/Norma User-Agent strings. We’ve even written rules for them. But these cover tiny parts of a framework’s functionality, not the attacks it can orchestrate.

An IP address, webshell or exploit used in a campaign doesn’t suddenly become an “ARTEX indicator” because ARTEX was involved.

And that’s why I find all these “ARTEX IoC collections” and “How to detect ARTEX” guides so misleading. They encourage people to think we’re dealing with another recognizable malware or C2 framework.

We’re facing a different class of offensive technology, and I think many people still haven’t understood that.

The detection guidance should be what we’ve been telling defenders for decades: detect malicious behavior, attack techniques and traces of compromise.

There is no special defense against ARTEX. Tomorrow the same attacker could use a different framework, a different model and completely different tools.

The names are disposable. The underlying attack techniques are what we need to detect.

B) ユーザのSSOで新しい端末を登録する

items.content:
Couldn't agree more! A single network detection rule won't be enough to address AI-assisted attacks.

An AI agent doesn't necessarily follow a fixed execution path. If Nmap fails, it can generate a Python scanner. If an HTTP request gets blocked, it can modify its approach or switch tools while pursuing the same objective.

We've already seen threat actors experimenting with multiple AI models, assigning different roles to agents, and adapting their operations based on feedback.

Static signatures still have value, but detecting the behavior across the entire attack sequence becomes much more important.

RT @IntCyberDigest: ‼️ On a Mac, a German "ß" in a file name can slip past security checks in popular developer tools. US vulnerability centre CERT/CC warned today.

Macs can treat "ß" and "ss" as the same file. Tools from Terraform and Deno to Python's setuptools compared the letters exactly, so a blocked file gets through under the other spelling.

A local attacker could overwrite protected files or sneak secrets into uploads and software packages.

Several vendors have assigned CVEs and shipped fixes.
